paragraphs.text: In Magic: The Gathering , colorless has two in-game meanings. It is either a type of objects or a type of mana . Note that colorless is not a color , and is not represented in the color wheel .
Being colorless can occur in three different senses, each of which has different implications for flavor and mechanics.

An object (a card or spell ) with no colored mana symbols in their mana costs is colorless. Lands, having no mana costs, are always colorless by default, with the sole exception of the color-indicated. Artifacts are the most common colorless spells, and Eldrazi creatures were made colorless to mark them as alien, with multiple associated noncreature spells. Karn and Ugin are colorless planeswalkers . In Strixhaven: School of Mages , several colorless Sorceries were printed as first-year introduction spells, in contrast to the colored school faculties.

The majority of colorless cards have generic mana costs, making them generalists allowed in any deck. Cards explicitly requiring colorless mana are most distinct, requiring decks to reliably produce uncommon mana to support them and emphasizing the colorless flavor.

Devoid is a characteristic-defining keyword ability that states that a card is colorless, regardless of the colors in that card's mana cost . All devoid cards are from Battle for Zendikar block and Modern Horizons 3 . Devoid cards have colored mana requirements, thus are often treated as if they were that color in design and gameplay role, but with special flavor and certain mechanical interactions due to lack of color.

Colorless cards come before colored cards in collector number , in contrast to artifacts and lands, which are numbered at the end of the set. Colorless cards that aren't artifacts or lands feature a transparent frame , allowing the art to run all the way to the border.

Artifacts can have mechanics usually reserved for a specific color, but typically with higher mana value or more complex conditions than that color would've required. This " jack of all trades , master of none" design pattern trades off efficiency for flexibility. For instance, colorless equipment can grant otherwise color-exclusive effects to any deck, but for more mana than an equivalent colored aura . Artifacts can also have unique strengths: For example, equipment improves on auras by surviving the death of the creature it's attached to.

Colorless cards that aren't artifacts or lands feature a transparent frame, allowing the art to run to the border. The primary cards to feature this frame are Eldrazi and spells related to them, though a few non-Eldrazi creatures and other spells feature this frame as well. Karn and Ugin planeswalkers feature colorless planeswalker frames.

Although colorless mana sources exist, colorless is not a color. Requiring colorless mana ( ) is as close as Magic comes to having a "sixth color" in tournament-legal gameplay, but there are few such cards - most colorless cards are either lands , or cost only generic mana , allowing them to be easily included in any deck. Every major card type can claim at least a few generic-cost cards, although the vast majority of them are artifacts .
Colorless gets access to pretty much everything, but at inefficient mana costs . For example, the destruction of permanents costs a minimum of .

Many more effects care about cards being lands or artifacts than care about lacking color. Lands in particular tend to be categorized separately from all other spells, even colorless ones, in their mechanics, design, and role in decks. However, some cards do address colorlessness directly, especially as a representative attribute for interacting with set themes like the Eldrazi, face-down permanents, or artifacts.

Artifacts can have mechanics usually reserved for a specific color, but typically with higher mana value or more complex conditions than that color would've required. This " jack of all trades , master of none" design pattern trades off efficiency for flexibility. For instance, colorless equipment can grant otherwise color-exclusive effects to any deck, but for more mana than an equivalent colored aura . Artifacts can also have unique strengths: For example, equipment improves on auras by surviving the death of the creature it's attached to. Other mechanics connected with artifacts include modular , sunburst , and crew .

Cards explicitly using colorless mana, as well as those with devoid , are not inherently associated with specific mechanics, but they can appear alongside "a colorless tribe's" abilities, such as the Eldrazi 's annihilator and ingest . Devoid cards' colored mana costs also give them access to mechanics in the appropriate slice of the color pie.
Colorless mana ( ) has no color .

The idea of colorless mana was already introduced in Limited Edition Alpha with Basalt Monolith , Mana Vault , and Sol Ring . It set the premise that most mana comes in one of the five colors ( white , blue , black , red , or green ), but there is a sixth subset of mana that is not any color. This mana could only be used to pay for costs that don't require color (for example, artifacts ).

In early sets, the text for Sol Ring was still spelled out as "Add 2 colorless mana to your mana pool". However, from Onslaught onwards, this was officially changed for editing reasons to "Add to your mana pool".

The cost of many cards includes generic mana (e.g., , ), meaning that a player can use that number of any mana (colored or colorless) to pay for it. Though one can use colorless mana to pay for generic mana costs, they are not the same thing. Generic is a type of cost, whereas colorless is a type of mana; a player cannot produce generic mana and, originally, there were no colorless costs . The latter changed with Oath of the Gatewatch .

R&D concluded that they had to stop using the mana circle with a number to represent both generic and colorless mana. Changing the representation of colorless mana was easier, as it's represented far less, so they decided to make the new mana symbol that represents one colorless mana. In our example the text for Sol Ring now is "Add ". One of the consequences of introducing a colorless mana symbol was the change to over 300 cards in Oracle , the central database of official card wordings.

As a consequence of the enduring and prolific Modern Urzatron strategy, two cards from Modern Horizons 2 specifically hate on lands that produce , in contrast to referring to lands that produce colored mana, which no cards do.

While adding colorless mana to your mana pool is an evergreen mechanic, colorless mana costs are not. Mana costs that can only be paid with colorless mana were first introduced in Oath of the Gatewatch and have yet to return to Premier sets. They do appear on new cards in the Eldrazi Unbound Commander Masters deck and in Modern Horizons 3 , however.

In the vision design of The Brothers' War , R&D did spend some time talking about whether they wanted to use colorless mana as a cost (similar to Oath of the Gatewatch ). They even went so far as to explore the idea of having fifteen draft archetypes with colorless mana filling the role of a sixth "color." In the end, it just didn't feel right.

In Marvel Super Heroes , Thanos, the Mad Titan is strongly associated with uniting the six Infinity Stones, which Magic represents through a power-up ability with an activation cost of . This was the first time a colorless cost was printed in a premier set in over a decade.

Unlike the five colors, colorless has no single unifying philosophy. Colorless cards can be flavored in a variety of ways. They can represent flexibility, in the sense of neutrality and the ability to work with any other color.

Since the majority of artifacts are tools rather than living entities or active magical spells, a lack of color in these cases is associated with science and technology over magic, and/or a lack of internal lifeforce or agency.

The Eldrazi are native to the Blind Eternities , traveling from plane to plane with ceaseless hunger, devouring their mana and life energy until their destruction. This sapping of energy drains its magical color and leaves behind Wastes , which produce colorless mana. The Eldrazi's colorless nature is connected with their ancient, alien origin as well as the specific form of devastation they cause.

The elder dragon planeswalker Ugin is also colorless, which (like the Eldrazi) is tied with his ancientness and special brand of magic, but in his case, is about transcendence beyond the colors rather than draining or disconnection from them. Accordingly, he uses colorless magic that works with the colors rather than rejecting colored mana, like concealment magic or his Ghostfire .
In Strixhaven: School of Mages , colorless Lessons depict basic courses that all students must take regardless of college .
In Avatar: The Last Airbender , depictions of the Avatar state are colorless to signify its transcendent, otherworldly nature.
The Wall tokens created by Invisible Woman and Invisible Woman, Sue Storm are colorless to represent their invisibility.
